summary: This bill amends the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 to expand SNAP eligibility to students with a student aid index of zero or less and certain independent students, while removing a restriction on counting educational loans as income and adjusting work requirements to include time spent attending college.

scores.thoughts: The bill expands SNAP eligibility to additional categories of higher-education students (those with a student aid index ≤ $0 and certain independent students) by repealing a restrictive paragraph in Section 5(k) and adding new qualifying criteria in Section 6(e). This directly increases the number of benefit recipients and therefore federal outlays on SNAP. The legislation therefore pushes in the direction of expanded government spending.
The bill contains no provisions altering tax rates, credits, deductions, or revenue measures of any kind.
No provisions address health insurance, Medicaid, Medicare, public option, or market-based health-care delivery.
No provisions relate to firearms, background checks, or gun regulations.
No provisions alter immigration pathways, border enforcement, or immigrant eligibility rules beyond the existing SNAP framework.
No provisions address reproductive health services or abortion access.
No provisions affect defense authorizations or military spending levels.
No provisions address environmental regulations, emissions standards, or conservation programs.

By broadening SNAP eligibility for low-income college students, the bill directly expands access to a core federal nutrition-assistance program that functions as part of the social safety net. This constitutes a clear expansion of welfare benefits.

While the bill references the Higher Education Act’s student-aid-index calculation and independent-student criteria, its purpose and mechanism are to adjust SNAP eligibility rules rather than to appropriate education funds, alter federal education policy, or promote school choice. The education references are incidental to the nutrition-benefit change.
No provisions address drug scheduling, decriminalization, or enforcement.
No provisions alter sentencing, policing, or rehabilitation programs.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.
The bill increases mandatory spending but does not contain any debt-ceiling, deficit-reduction target, or PAYGO provisions; its primary focus is program expansion rather than fiscal consolidation.
No provisions address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance or international aid.
No provisions address voting access, voter ID, or election administration.
No provisions address data privacy, technology regulation, or surveillance.
No provisions address collective bargaining, union rights, or employer obligations.
No provisions address religious exemptions or anti-discrimination rules.

The bill expands SNAP eligibility to more college students (those with zero or negative student aid index and certain independent students), directly increasing mandatory federal spending on nutrition assistance with no offsets, revenue measures, or cuts elsewhere. This spending expansion is the sole purpose of the legislation.
